title: Mid-term exam: loops, conditions, arrays and strings
overview: These are Shammunul's answers to the mid-term exam problems. Each one is short, but together they test everything up to this point: nested loops, `if / else if` chains, reading arrays, counting with a condition, stopping early with `break`, and comparing strings with `strcmp`. They are good for revision because each one uses a single clear pattern.

concepts.explain: Most solutions read all `N` values into an array in one loop, then work on them in a second loop. Keeping the two jobs apart makes the logic easier to follow.
Start a counter at 0 and add 1 each time a value passes the test. A range test has two sides: `x >= X && x <= Y`.

concepts.term: Running total with an early stop
concepts.explain: Keep adding values to a total. The first time the total goes past the limit, `break`, because the list is sorted and later values are even bigger.
Check the ranges in order so that each value falls into exactly one branch. Put the catch-all case in the final `else`.
Strings can't be compared with `<`. Use `strcmp`, and use `strcpy` to save the current best string.
Limits such as `10^9`, or sums of many values, can overflow a 32-bit `int`. Use `long long` with `%lld`.

files.title: Print 1..K, N times
files.what: Prints the row `1 2 ... K` a total of `N` times. It is a basic nested loop.
steps: Read `N` (how many rows) and `K` (how far each row counts).
The outer loop `i` runs `N` times, once for each row.
The inner loop `j` goes from 1 to `K` and prints each number followed by a space.
After the inner loop, `printf("\n")` ends the row.
files.input_note: N = 3 rows, K = 4 numbers per row.
files.output_note: Three lines of `1 2 3 4 `. Each line ends with a space, which judges usually accept.
files.watch_out: Put the newline outside the inner loop. Inside it, every number would land on its own line.

check.q: How many numbers are printed in total for input `7 4`?

files.title: Classify candidates by experience
files.what: For each experience value, prints one of four labels. It is an `if / else if` chain over number ranges.
steps: Read `N`, then `N` experience values into `experiences`.
For each value: below 1 is `Entry-level`.
From 1 to 3 is `Junior`, and from 4 to 7 is `Mid-level`.
Anything left (above 7) falls into the final `else` and is `Senior`.
files.output_note: One label per line, in input order: Entry-level, Junior, Mid-level, Senior, Junior.
files.watch_out: The `>= 1` and `>= 4` checks aren't needed, because the earlier branches already ruled those values out. They are harmless, though.

files.title: Lexicographic min and max of 3 strings
files.what: Finds the string that comes first and the one that comes last in dictionary order. It uses the same pattern as min/max of three numbers, with `strcmp` in place of `<`.
steps: Read the three words into `S1`, `S2` and `S3`.
Copy `S1` into both `min` and `max` as the starting guess.
If `strcmp(S2, min) < 0`, then `S2` comes earlier, so copy it into `min`. Do the same check for `S3`.
If `strcmp(S2, max) > 0`, then `S2` comes later, so copy it into `max`. Do the same check for `S3`.
Print `min`, then `max`, each on its own line.
files.complexity: Time O(L) where L is string length · Space O(L)
files.input_note: Three lowercase words on one line.
files.watch_out: `min = S2` does not compile for arrays. Use `strcpy`. The arrays are sized 1001 to leave room for `'\0'`.

check.q: What does `strcmp("cat", "car")` return: a negative number, zero or a positive number?
check.a: A positive number, because `t` comes after `r`.

files.title: Count prices inside a range
files.what: Counts the phones whose price is between `X` and `Y`, including both ends.
steps: Read `N`, `X` and `Y`. `X` and `Y` are `long long` because prices can reach 10^9.
Read the `N` prices into `prices`.
Loop over them and add 1 to `count` when `prices[i] >= X && prices[i] <= Y`.
Print `count`.
files.input_note: 6 prices, and the range is 10 to 20.
files.output_note: `4`: the prices 10, 15, 20 and 12 are inside the range. Both ends count.
files.watch_out: `long long prices[100000]` takes about 800 KB inside `main`. It fits here, but making big arrays global is safer.

check.q: What would the answer be if the check used `>` and `<` instead?
check.a: 2 (only 15 and 12), because the prices 10 and 20 would be left out.

files.title: How many books fit in T time
files.what: The reading times are sorted from shortest to longest, so reading the shortest books first gives the most books. The program keeps a running total and stops at the first book that doesn't fit.
steps: Read `N`, `T` and the `N` sorted times.
`total_time` adds up the time of each book in order.
While `total_time <= T`, add 1 to `number_of_books`.
The first time the total goes past `T`, `break`. Every later book is at least as long, so none of them can fit either.
Print `number_of_books`.
files.input_note: 6 books and 20 minutes. The times are already sorted.
files.output_note: `4`: 2+3+5+7 = 17 fits, but adding 11 makes 28, which is more than 20.
files.watch_out: `total_time` is `long long`. The sum of 10^5 times can pass the `int` limit.

check.q: With `T = 0`, what does the program print?
check.a: 0. The first book already takes more than 0 time (all times are positive), so the loop breaks at once.

recap: Nested loops: the outer loop counts rows, and the inner loop prints what goes in each row.
Range checks use `&&` and must include or exclude the ends exactly as the problem says.
On sorted data, a running total plus `break` answers "how many fit".
Compare strings with `strcmp` and copy them with `strcpy`.
Use `long long` when values or sums can pass about 2×10^9.

check_yourself.q: Why does taking the books in the given order give the most books?
check_yourself.a: The list is sorted, so the shortest books come first. Any other choice uses at least as much time for the same number of books.

check_yourself.q: In an `if / else if` chain, why is the last case usually a plain `else`?
check_yourself.a: Everything that didn't match earlier belongs there, so no extra condition is needed.

check_yourself.q: Why can't you write `if (s1 < s2)` for two C strings?
check_yourself.a: That compares the two array addresses, not the text. Use `strcmp(s1, s2) < 0`.

body: This page is the mid-term, and the calmest way into it is to notice that nothing on it is new. Every problem is a pattern you have already written, dressed in a short story about books, phones or job applicants.

Here is the whole toolbox the exam mixes. Read `n` values into an array. Walk the array and do one small thing per value. Count the values that pass a test. Keep a running total and stop early. Sort values into named groups with `if / else if`. Print rows with a loop inside a loop. Compare and copy words with `strcmp` and `strcpy`. That is all of it, and each answer below uses one of them.

Four of the five answers have the same shape, so that is the one to have in your fingers: read everything first, then process. The first loop does nothing clever, it only fills the array. The second loop holds the actual question.
Say the prices are `5 10 15 20 25 12` and you have to count the ones between 10 and 20, with both ends included. The second loop asks one question per price and adds 1 when the answer is yes.
Change the single line in the middle and the same skeleton answers something else: add to a total instead of counting, or print a label instead of adding.
intro.trace:
price    in 10..20 ?    count
   5         no             0
  10         yes            1
  15         yes            2
  20         yes            3
  25         no             3
  12         yes            4

body: **A running total that stops early.** The reading times of the books arrive already sorted from shortest to longest, so taking them in the given order is the best you can do. Add them up one at a time and stop at the first book that does not fit, because every later book is at least as long and cannot fit either. With 20 minutes and the times `2 3 5 7 11 13` the answer is 4.

**Named ranges.** An `if / else if` chain drops each value into exactly one group. Write the ranges in order, and let the last case be a plain `else` so that everything the earlier tests missed lands there without another condition.
intro.trace:
time   total   total <= 20 ?   books
  2       2         yes            1
  3       5         yes            2
  5      10         yes            3
  7      17         yes            4
 11      28         no          -> stop

body: **Min and max, but with words.** You have found the smallest of three numbers before: keep the first one as the current best, then replace it whenever you meet something smaller. Words work the same way with two substitutions. `a < b` becomes `strcmp(a, b) < 0`, and `best = s` becomes `strcpy(best, s)`, because one array cannot be assigned to another.

**Rows.** Printing the numbers 1 to `k` a total of `n` times is a loop inside a loop. The inner loop prints one row, and the `printf("\n")` belongs after it rather than inside it, or every number ends up on a line of its own.

What to watch for under exam pressure, roughly in the order it costs marks. Read the required output format twice, because capitals, spaces and new lines are compared character by character. Check whether a range includes its ends: `>=` and `<=` against `>` and `<` is the difference between the answers 4 and 2 in the price problem. Size an array from the constraint in the statement, not from the sample. And when a single value can reach 10^9, or a sum piles up 100000 of them, use `long long` and print it with `%lld`.
The five answers below are short on purpose. Read each one as an example of its pattern rather than as a problem to memorise, and the next exam will look like the same handful of questions again.
